messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Tran is a 38-year-old Vietnamese American stockbroker who presented for psychological assessment reporting significant distress in the wake of a prolonged stalking ordeal that ended approximately fourteen months ago. She is currently in a relationship and describes her partner as supportive, though she acknowledges that her difficulties have begun to strain their life together in ways she can no longer minimize.

The stalking began three years ago and escalated over the course of eighteen months. The perpetrator, a former professional acquaintance, initially made contact through her firm's public-facing channels before his behavior grew progressively more intrusive. What Linh remembers most vividly — and what she finds most destabilizing to recall — is a night he appeared outside her apartment building. He had been drinking; she could smell the alcohol on him from several feet away as he blocked the entrance, speaking in a low, controlled voice that somehow frightened her more than shouting would have. A family was crossing the street nearby — a couple with two young children, laughing at something — and she remembers registering them with a kind of desperate envy, feeling utterly removed from that ordinary world. He was eventually removed by a neighbor who called the police, but not before Linh had stood frozen in the cold for what felt like an hour. It was the closest he had ever come to her physically, and it is the memory that has lodged most deeply.

What makes the memory itself so disorienting is its quality. Linh describes it as something that still does not feel entirely real — the scene is so extreme, so far outside the life she had built, that some part of her cannot fully accept it as her own history. And yet when the memory surfaces, the unreality offers no protection. She does not experience it as something distant or dreamlike; she experiences it as immediate. When it comes — unbidden, in the middle of a trading floor conversation or while reviewing a client portfolio — she feels the cold air, the particular quality of his voice, the paralysis in her chest. The terror she felt that night returns with a fidelity that leaves her shaking, her heart rate spiking, her hands momentarily useless on the keyboard. It is not a recollection so much as a reinstatement.

It is precisely because the memory carries such sensory and emotional force that certain features of ordinary life have become impossible to navigate without distress. The memory, when activated, seems to reach forward and charge the world around her with threat. The smell of alcohol — from a colleague's breath at a work function, from a glass left on a conference table — can collapse the distance between now and then in an instant, pulling her back into that doorway with a vividness she cannot interrupt. Loud noises on the trading floor, the sudden slam of a door or a burst of shouting from a nearby desk, carry the same destabilizing force; they do not merely startle her but seem to confirm that danger is close. And perhaps most unexpectedly, the sight of happy families — couples with children in the park near her office, the kind of ordinary tableau she had observed that night — has become quietly unbearable. She had come to believe that such images mark the distance between herself and a life she can no longer access, and encountering them now pulls at something raw.

Over the past year, Linh has restructured her days around avoiding these triggers where possible. She takes different routes to work, declines client dinners where alcohol will be present, and has begun eating lunch alone at her desk rather than risk the unpredictability of a restaurant. A senior colleague recently commented on her withdrawal, and she was passed over for a team leadership role that she suspects was contingent on the kind of visible, sociable presence she can no longer sustain. Her partner has noticed the absences — the evenings she spends rigid and silent, the weekends she will not leave the apartment. What finally brought her to seek help was not a single crisis but the accumulating weight of a life grown smaller. What she is most afraid of is that the memory will never stop feeling like the present. What she is most hoping for is to be able to smell the air outside her own building without bracing for something that already happened.
